Chapter 27

The map with no tile server

svelte-maplibre over MapLibre GL: a style built from the prerendered world, a worker URL set once in a module script, great-circle legs as a GeoJSON line layer, draggable markers, a theme-following style patched with diffStyleUpdates, and geolocation through createSubscriber.

By the end of this chapter

Put an interactive vector map in a SvelteKit app that works offline, in CI and under a strict CSP, and wire its state in and out of Svelte.

The map is where most trip planners send you to a tile provider, an API key and a connect-src that names somebody else’s domain. This one draws every country from a bundled atlas and needs none of that. What it costs is streets, and at the scale a trip is planned — a country, a coastline, a city as a dot — that is the right trade for a project that has to work on a train and in CI.

A MapLibre style is JSON: sources and layers. One GeoJSON source, the prerendered /api/world.json from chapter 16, and three layers — sea, land, borders. No sprite, no glyphs, because no layer draws text. The colours are literals rather than tokens, and the comment says why: MapLibre paints a canvas and does not read the cascade, so mapPalette() holds the five colours each scheme needs — the route is --sea copied by hand, one of the four hand copies the header of tokens.css lists, each where a custom property cannot reach — worldStyle() builds the style from them, and the component reads the same palette for the route and rebuilds the style when the theme flips. The comment also says exactly what to change to put OpenFreeMap tiles under it — one source and one CSP line.

The component

MapLibre parses geometry in a Web Worker, and Vite has to be told to emit that worker as a file — ?worker&url does — and MapLibre has to be handed the URL once, before the first map. A <script module> runs once per module, not once per instance, which is exactly the place. The CSP’s worker-src "self" blob: in chapter 03 is for this file.

The route is one great-circle line per leg — arc() from the library, forty-eight segments, unwrapped across the date line — as a GeoJSON FeatureCollection the LineLayer draws. fit is the padded bounds from the same library. diffStyleUpdates makes MapLibre patch three paint properties when the theme flips rather than tear the map down. bind:map hands the underlying Map instance back for the imperative calls, the first of them fitBounds on a button — which fits the route into the part of the canvas that is on screen: the side-by-side map is as tall as the viewport under the sticky tabs, so at the top of the page its bottom is below the fold, and the hidden strip is counted as padding.

The route is framed once, as a cut, when the map has loaded and there is a route to frame — and after that the camera belongs to the person. It moves for “Fit the route”, for a bubble pressed and for a stop chosen, and for nothing else. The effect that frames it is written so that it can only ever do so once: framed is a plain let, and once it is true the effect returns before it has read anything reactive, so it has no dependencies left and never runs again.

Why not bounds={fit} on <MapLibre>

Because svelte-maplibre re-fits the map whenever bounds changes, and fit is derived from the stops — which the live query hands over as a new array every time anybody’s heartbeat wakes the room. Choosing a stop sends a heartbeat. So the flight to the chosen stop took off, the next snapshot arrived a few frames later, and the whole route was fitted again underneath it: on the desktop’s side map, choosing Sagrada Família left the camera on the overview with its pin about 155px from the middle. A prop that is “the bounds to show” is right for a map whose view is a pure function of its data; this one is not, because a person moves it.

The second effect is a repair for something MapLibre does not do reliably. It watches its own container and redraws the canvas when the container changes size — but on a phone the frame’s height is measured from the trip’s header after the map has started, and in five loads out of six the canvas was redrawn for the new height while every pin stayed where the old height had put them: 25px below the route, until something moved the camera. So the frame is watched here too, and a change of size asks for resize() again — at once if the camera is still, or on the moveend of the move in progress. At rest, resize() redraws and re-places every marker, which is all the cure needs to know about the cause. The first report a ResizeObserver makes is the size it started at, not a change, and is let go. TripView also guesses the header’s height per width now, so in the usual case there is no change of size to repair.

Five Lisbon stops at the zoom that fits Lisbon to Barcelona are one blob of pins with only the top number readable. So markers that would share a press are drawn as one bubble that says which numbers it holds — “1–5” for a run of the route, “3, 5” or “1–5, 12” when a city is visited at two points of it — and pressing it fits the camera to them. “Would share a press” is the same 44px the phone’s target check presses with: two press areas that touch are two targets a finger cannot tell apart, however they are drawn. A press area is 44px square, or as wide as the marker when the marker is wider, and a bubble’s width is guessed from its label, generously, because the grouping has to be decided before there is anything drawn to measure.

The trick that makes it cheap is that the test needs no screen. A point’s Web Mercator coordinate, 0 to 1 across the world, times 512 × 2^zoom is where MapLibre draws it in world pixels at that zoom, and two stops 44 of those apart are 44 screen pixels apart wherever the map is panned — so the grouping is a $derived of the stops, the zoom and the selection. bind:zoom is written by svelte-maplibre on moveend, so the groups are recomputed once per gesture, not on every frame of it. Any two markers that touch are merged, the merged bubble moves to the middle of what it holds, and the loop runs again until no two touch — because a bubble that has grown and moved may now touch a neighbour it did not.

Two exceptions keep it honest. The selected stop is never folded into a bubble — the one thing a person asked to see is always a pin — and above zoom 16 nothing is grouped, because two stops that close are on the same street and a bubble there would never come apart. The label lists numbers rather than counting them because a count lied: a bubble holding stops 3 and 5 said “2”, beside the pin that *is* stop 2; only past two runs of numbers does the count come back. The bubble is a button whose name is its label plus a visually hidden “2 stops here, zoom in”, in the page’s language; the stop names are only its title, and a single pin is named by its number. The bubble’s first draft spelled its stops out in that hidden text, which made a second button called “Alfama” beside the itinerary’s own, and every test that asked for “the Alfama button” found two.

And a stop chosen is a stop shown. Selecting one — in the list, in the palette, on the map — flies the camera to it, which also takes it out of any bubble; under reduced motion it is a jump. How close is a judgement about this atlas, which has coastlines and borders and nothing under them. A fixed street-level zoom put Alfama in an empty beige field; a fixed country-level one still showed no coast at Lisbon and hid the hotel a kilometre away under the chosen pin. What tells a person where a stop is, at the scale of a city, is the trip’s other stops around it, so closeEnough() works out the zoom at which the chosen pin’s press area — a quarter larger while it is chosen — touches no other stop’s, from the same world-pixel arithmetic as the bubbles, and the camera goes there: never further out than zoom 9, never closer than 16, and never out from where the map already is.

flownTo is a plain let, not $state, on purpose: it is what the effect writes down about where it went, and an effect that depended on its own note would run again for having written it. The zoom is read with untrack for the same reason — a flight changes the zoom, and the effect must not answer its own flight. round() keeps five decimal places, a metre, on every coordinate the map hands over: the map’s click and a dragged pin give fifteen, which nobody typed and no field shows.

For an editor, a click on empty map starts a new stop there — and for a while a click on a pin or a bubble did too. Pressing a bubble asked for a zoom and got the “New stop” dialog over it. The marker’s own click handler calls stopPropagation(), and it comes too late: MapLibre listens for clicks on the element the markers live in, with addEventListener, and the marker’s handler is a Svelte onclick, which Svelte *delegates* — it attaches one listener at the root of the app and runs the handlers on the event’s path when the event arrives there. By then the click has already passed MapLibre on its way up. So the map’s own handler asks where the click began, and a click that began inside .maplibregl-marker is not a click on the map.

Why the map checks the target instead of the marker stopping the event

Because the marker’s handler is not ours — it is inside svelte-maplibre — and the fix that would work there, a native listener in the capture phase, is the kind of fight with the framework’s event model the Svelte documentation warns about: a stopPropagation() in a hand-added listener keeps the event from ever reaching the root, and every delegated handler above it silently stops working. Asking the event where it started is local, cannot break anybody else’s handler, and reads as what it means.

svelte-maplibre’s components are thin and declarative: <GeoJSON> is a source, <LineLayer> a layer inside it, <Marker> a DOM element positioned by the map. The route is two layers over one source — a wide halo in the paper colour, then the dashed line on top — so the dashes read where they cross a border. onload sets data-ready, which the CSS turns into a fade-in, so the canvas never flashes an empty frame. Markers are asButton so they are focusable, draggable when the viewer may edit, and the pin inside is ours — numbered, coloured by kind through the same --kind property the card uses, and scaled when selected. The selected marker carries zIndex={10}: pins that share a city paint in list order, and a z-index on the pin inside cannot climb out of the marker’s own stacking context, so the ring around “1” used to show a “5”.

A pin is drawn 26px across and pressed across 44px, and the difference is a pseudo-element. The arithmetic has one trap, the same one the icon buttons fell into: an absolutely placed box is measured from its parent’s *padding* edge, inside the border, so a reach of (44 − 26) / 2 = 9px from the outside of a pin with a 2px ring made a 40px target. A percentage inset is a share of the padding box — of its width for the sides, its height for the top and bottom — so min(-2px, calc(50% - var(--control) / 2)) is right for both shapes at once: a round pin reaches out to 44px each way, and a bubble that is already wider than 44px reaches sideways only to its own ring, and does not grow into its neighbours. The phone’s target check in chapter 42 presses every marker at that distance.

Where am I, as a reactive value

createSubscriber from svelte/reactivity turns an external source of events into something a template can read like state. The function it is given runs when the value is first read inside an effect and its cleanup runs when nothing reads it any more — so the browser’s position watch starts the moment the template shows geo.fix and stops the moment it stops showing it. Nobody calls start; nobody forgets stop; the “Where am I” button toggles a boolean and the watch follows. That is the pattern for any subscription-shaped API — a BroadcastChannel, a ResizeObserver, a WebSocket — and chapter 40 returns to it.

Why svelte-maplibre and not the MapLibre API through an attachment

Because a map has a lot of *declarative* state — sources, layers, markers with positions — and a wrapper that turns those into components lets the itinerary’s stops become markers with an {#each}. An attachment would be right for the map instance itself and wrong for thirty markers that come and go. The line is: use a wrapper when the library’s objects map onto a tree the template already has; use an attachment when the library wants one element and owns it. Tiptap, in chapter 30, is the second case.

Checkpoint

  • You can say what the style contains, what it costs, and what one change would add tiles.
  • You can explain why the worker URL is set in a module script and which CSP line it needs.
  • You can describe createSubscriber and give one other API it would fit.
  • You can say how the map decides that two pins overlap without asking where they are on screen, and why the result is a $derived.
  • You can explain why a marker’s stopPropagation() did not keep its click from reaching the map, and what the map checks instead.
